clue.text: Frost to stop return of the pools

parts.note: Jack Frost is the personification of frosty weather

indicators.note: a return goes back the way it came, so the word stop is read backwards

parts.note: taken as written before it is turned round

explanation.surface: An order to halt the cold weather from coming back to the swimming baths.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return of' turns STOP into POTS. 'The pools' looks like swimming baths, but means the football pools, a British betting game.
explanation.definitionFit: Jackpots are the large accumulated prizes in a lottery-style competition such as the football pools.

clue.text: Justice according to Stone?

parts.note: J is the abbreviation for Justice, a judge's title
as per means according to

explanation.surface: Asks what the law says in the opinion of someone named Stone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stone' looks like a surname to follow 'Justice', but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Jasper is an opaque red or brown quartz, a semi-precious mineral.

clue.text: No one raised in Bordeaux makes an archaic form of instrument

indicators.note: the turned pieces go in the middle of the wine

parts.note: claret is red Bordeaux wine

indicators.note: in a down clue raised means read upwards, so the pieces are turned backwards

parts.note: taken as written
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Nobody in Bordeaux has heard of an old-fashioned woodwind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raised' suits a down clue, where the turned letters read upwards; 'Bordeaux' stands for its red wine, not the city.
explanation.definitionFit: Clarionet is an old spelling of the clarinet, the single-reed woodwind.

clue.text: After a time Frank must be paid

parts.note: post is Latin for after, as in postwar
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: Someone called Frank will be paid eventually.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frank' looks like a name; it is the stamp franking a letter. 'must be paid' rounds off the surface: postage is due.
explanation.definitionFit: A frank is a mark on mail showing the charge for sending it has been paid.

clue.text: Part of the National Trust perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps hints the letters could be arranged otherwise, so they are shuffled

parts.note: taken as written as fodder
NT is the abbreviation for the National Trust, the British heritage charity

explanation.surface: Something that belongs to Britain's heritage charity, maybe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges THE plus NT. The National Trust is Britain's charity that runs historic houses.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenth is one of ten equal portions of a whole.

clue.text: Result of flight of black convict?

parts.note: jet is a deep glossy black, as in jet-black
an old lag is slang for a habitual convict

explanation.surface: Asks what follows when a dark-skinned prisoner escapes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flight' suggests a convict fleeing; it is air travel. LAG is British slang for a prisoner.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiredness from crossing time zones is what a long air journey leaves you with.

clue.text: New car tire is unreliable

indicators.note: new suggests a fresh version, so these letters are reformed

parts.note: taken as written as fodder
taken as written as fodder

explanation.surface: A new tyre on the car proves unreliable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' rearranges CAR TIRE. 'Tire' is the American spelling of tyre.
explanation.definitionFit: Something erratic behaves unpredictably and cannot be depended upon.

clue.text: Flower of Charles Pooter's youth

definitions.meaning: a tall garden plant with spikes of blooms
Charles Pooter, hero of the Grossmiths' comic novel The Diary of a Nobody, has a young son

explanation.surface: A bloom from the days when a fictional clerk was young.
explanation.walkthrough: 'youth' seems to mean his early years; it is his son, a young man. The Diary of a Nobody is a classic English comic novel.
explanation.definitionFit: The garden plant shares its name with Pooter's son, the youngster of the family.

clue.text: Fuel-gauge shows meagrest outflow

indicators.note: an outflow pours the letters out in a new order

explanation.surface: A gauge shows only the slightest leak of fuel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outflow' rearranges MEAGREST.
explanation.definitionFit: A household meter records the volume of fuel supplied, so it gauges consumption.

clue.text: Held initially as plunder

parts.note: to pirate is to rob or plunder

explanation.surface: Someone captured at first as booty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Held initially' points to the start of 'Held', the H sound; an aspirate is a breathed consonant such as h.
explanation.definitionFit: The breathy h-sound that opens the word 'Held' is what phoneticians call an aspirate.

clue.text: Military insignia carried by staff in US

definitions.meaning: generals wear stars on their shoulders and sergeants wear stripes on their sleeves
the American national flag flies from a flagstaff

explanation.surface: Badges of rank worn by American army personnel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staff' suggests military personnel, but it is the pole a flag flies on.
explanation.definitionFit: Both ranks' badges together name the American flag, which is hoisted on a pole.

clue.text: Post mortem aide-mémoire

parts.note: read literally, post mortem means after death, and an aide-mémoire is a reminder: an inscription that keeps the dead in mind

explanation.surface: A pathologist's notes to self after an autopsy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Post mortem' suggests an autopsy, but here it is the Latin 'after death'.
explanation.definitionFit: A tombstone inscription is a memorial written after someone dies to recall them.

clue.text: Decimal point indicates extreme

parts.note: decimal counting proceeds in tens
E (east) is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: A remark that the decimal point marks something extreme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Decimal point' reads as one thing; split it. 'Decimal' gives IN TENS and 'point' is E, a compass point.
explanation.definitionFit: Intense feelings or heat are those of extreme strength.

clue.text: Submarine endures a disaster

indicators.note: a disaster throws things into chaos, so these letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder
taken as written

explanation.surface: A submarine survives a catastrophe at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disaster' rearranges ENDURES A. 'Submarine' looks like a noun but is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something lying or happening beneath the surface of the sea.

clue.text: NY battle scene in story about desert love

indicators.note: the story wraps around the other pieces

parts.note: a saga is a long story
to rat is to desert or betray
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A tale of romance in the desert set at a New York battlefield.
explanation.walkthrough: 'desert' looks like a noun but is the verb, to abandon; 'love' as O comes from the tennis score.
explanation.definitionFit: Saratoga in New York State was the site of a decisive 1777 battle in the American War of Independence.

clue.text: Hide the money? Sound idea

indicators.note: here sound means spoken aloud, so the money's word is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: cash is money in notes and coins

explanation.surface: Suggests that stashing your savings away is a wise plan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound idea' reads as 'good plan'; 'Sound' is the homophone signal, and 'idea' rounds off the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: To cache something is to stow it away in a secret store.

clue.text: Inner coil arrangement for outstanding fashion

indicators.note: an arrangement puts the letters into a new order

parts.note: taken as written as fodder
taken as written as fodder

explanation.surface: An internal spring arranged for a striking style of dress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arrangement' rearranges INNER COIL. 'Outstanding' means literally standing out.
explanation.definitionFit: A hooped petticoat made skirts stand out widely, a Victorian fashion.

clue.text: A security case involving drink

parts.note: reads like a criminal investigation about alcohol, but describes a lockable stand holding decanters

explanation.surface: A police inquiry into alcohol and safety.
explanation.walkthrough: The stand is named after the mythical king tormented by drink just out of reach, as the decanters are visible but locked.
explanation.definitionFit: This lockable stand displays decanters of spirits while keeping them secure from servants.

clue.text: Shape of Grecian urn hailed by Keats

definitions.text: Shape of Grecian urn hailed by Keats

parts.words: Shape of Grecian urn hailed by Keats
parts.note: Keats's Ode on a Grecian Urn addresses the vase with the cry 'O ... shape!', using the adjective for classical Athens

explanation.surface: Recalls the romantic poet's praise for an ancient vase.
explanation.walkthrough: The ode's final stanza opens 'O Attic shape! Fair attitude!'; the word means Athenian, though it also suggests a loft.
explanation.definitionFit: Attic means of ancient Athens, the classical Greek style the poet praised in the urn.

clue.text: Prime Minister's means of preservation

definitions.meaning: George ... was briefly British premier in 1827
putting food into sealed tins keeps it

explanation.surface: Describes how a premier keeps himself going.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: George Canning led the British government in 1827; sealing food in tins is a way to keep it.

clue.text: "Trivial" oratory

definitions.meaning: read literally, belonging to the trivium, the medieval course of grammar, logic and one more art
the art of persuasive public speaking

explanation.surface: A dismissive view of speechmaking as unimportant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trivial' seems to mean petty, but the quotation marks ask for its root sense: part of the trivium, the three medieval liberal arts.
explanation.definitionFit: The art of eloquent persuasion was one of the three subjects of the medieval trivium.

clue.text: New order is boost for players

indicators.note: a new order of letters means they are reshuffled

parts.note: taken as written as fodder
taken as written as fodder

explanation.surface: A fresh system gives the musicians a lift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New order' rearranges IS BOOST.
explanation.definitionFit: Oboists are musicians who perform on the double-reed woodwind.

clue.text: Note produced by singer, say

indicators.note: say signals a word as spoken, so the singer's word is heard not spelt

parts.note: a tenor is a high male singer

explanation.surface: A high musical note sung by a vocalist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Note' suggests music, but it is a ten-pound banknote, British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: A ten-pound banknote is called this in British slang.

clue.text: It's the highest bird that makes the crest

parts.note: the top is the highest part
the knot is a wading bird of the sandpiper family

explanation.surface: The bird perched highest earns the title of crest.
explanation.walkthrough: A knot is a small shorebird, a crossword favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: A tuft or knot of hair or ribbons on the crown of the head is a crest.

clue.text: Top academician goes to party in the gallery

parts.note: PRA stands for President of the Royal Academy, Britain's leading arts institution
a do is a party

explanation.surface: The head of the Royal Academy attends a reception at an art museum.
explanation.walkthrough: PRA is President of the Royal Academy of Arts in London.
explanation.definitionFit: The Prado in Madrid is Spain's national art museum.

clue.text: Suggest work in non-metrical form

indicators.note: the word for work sits in the middle of the word for non-metrical form

parts.note: prose is writing without metre
op, short for opus, is a musical work

explanation.surface: Advice to write in prose rather than verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'non-metrical form' means writing without metre, the opposite of verse.
explanation.definitionFit: To propose is to put forward an idea for consideration.

clue.text: One of the fruits of cut-back?

definitions.meaning: to trim a shrub by lopping its branches

explanation.surface: Asks what a harsh trim on a tree yields.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of' is a link word between the two definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: A dried plum is a familiar fruit; to trim branches is to do this to a plant.

clue.text: Bridge player's problem do we hear in cross-examination?

definitions.meaning: at bridge the player on lead must decide which card to play first
a barrister's question that prompts the witness towards the desired reply

explanation.surface: A card player's dilemma, and what courtroom listeners hear.
explanation.walkthrough: In bridge, leading means playing the first card of a trick.
explanation.definitionFit: Bridge: deciding which card to open with; law: a query worded to suggest its reply, often objected to in court.

clue.text: Southern Irish lake is a quagmire

parts.note: lough is the Irish word for a lake, like Scottish loch

explanation.surface: A lake in the south of Ireland turns out to be boggy.
explanation.walkthrough: Slough here rhymes with 'cow', a muddy swamp; it is also an English town.
explanation.definitionFit: A slough is a muddy hollow or swamp, a bog to get stuck in.

clue.text: Do people curse morning dress, for example?

parts.note: men means people in general, as in all men
to swear is to curse

explanation.surface: Asks whether folk grumble at the formal wedding outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Do' is a link word. Morning dress is the British formal tailcoat outfit worn at weddings and Ascot.
explanation.definitionFit: Morning dress is a formal outfit for gentlemen, so it is an instance of male clothing.
